recall_prompt: Say how you would find both sets — what the operation acts on, and which pairs survive the square root.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Add 2 to each image
steps.margin_note: One mark. These operations act on the SECOND coordinate only — the inputs never change.
steps.memory_tip: These operations act on the SECOND coordinate only — the inputs never change.

recall.must_convey: That 2 is added to each image (the second coordinate), leaving the first coordinates untouched: {(1,4), (2,−1), (3,1)}.
accept: add two to each second value so you get one four two minus one and three one
the inputs stay the same and two is added to every image
two plus f is one comma four two comma minus one three comma one
second coordinate ki two add cheyyali inputs marave
add two to each output only

steps.why: An operation on a function acts on its outputs. The domain is fixed by the pairs already there, so the first coordinates cannot move.
common_mistakes: Adding 2 to the first coordinate as well, which changes the domain.

steps.label: Take the square root of each image
steps.margin_note: The second mark. Only the images that are non negative survive — the others are not real numbers, so those pairs are dropped.
steps.memory_tip: Only non-negative images survive √f. The pairs with negative values are dropped, not made imaginary.

recall.must_convey: That the square root is taken of each image, and pairs whose image is negative are dropped because their roots are not real — leaving only {(1, √2)}.
accept: root of two is fine but root of minus three and root of minus one are not real so only one comma root two survives
drop the negative images because their square roots are not real numbers
only the pair with image two remains giving one comma root two
minus three and minus one negative kabatti real kaadu so oke pair migulutundi
square root f is just the single pair one comma root two

steps.why: √f is a real function only where the image is non negative, so the operation can shrink the domain — that is the whole point of this part.
common_mistakes: Keeping all three pairs and writing √−3 as an answer.
Writing the imaginary values instead of dropping the pairs.

insider_note: √f drops every pair whose image is negative, so two of the three pairs vanish and the answer is a SMALLER set. Writing √(−3) as a value is exactly the error this question is set to catch.
